notes: 2025-26 Topps Chrome base set, LA Lakers. Printed name is REAVES (not Reeves). Card is in a penny sleeve, photographed sideways, with glare across the right of the frame and a hard white/wood background edge that the quad detector could mistake for the card. The collector number is not on the front — expect it missing rather than wrong unless something invents one. No insert (base card), so `insert` is unasserted.

2025-26 Topps Chrome 'Ball of Duty' insert, Detroit Pistons. Same sleeve/rotation/glare conditions. Insert code BD11 is not on the front, but the insert name is printed large. Product goes in setName, treatment in insert.

2023-24 Donruss Rated Rookie, Memphis Grizzlies. First fixture in a rigid magnetic holder rather than a penny sleeve, first held in hand (fingers and a blurred room in frame rather than a flat surface), first non-Topps manufacturer, and first parallel. The parallel is the point: base and Red Laser Holo share name, set, number and year but are worth very different amounts, so missing it misprices the listing. Expect `parallel` to come back missing unless CardSight returns a trustworthy exact match — OCR has no field that reaches it. Name asserted with the 'II' suffix as printed; if catalogues return 'GG Jackson' this will score wrong, which is a decision to make on the evidence rather than by loosening matching up front. `cardNumber` unasserted (it is on the back). Donruss 'Rated Rookie' is the rookie designation for this product, so `rookie` is asserted as well as `insert` — the same banner carries both meanings, which is a good test of whether the two fields stay distinct.

FIRST GRADED SLAB and FIRST SCREENSHOT — this is a phone screenshot of an eBay listing page, not a photo of a card, so it tests something different from the rest. The card image sits small inside browser chrome, and the listing title ('2024 Obsidian Orbital Molten Gold /10 LEBRON JAMES #16 PSA 10 POP 2') is legible text in the frame, so a model can score well here by reading the page rather than the card. Treat a good result as evidence about screenshots, not about card reading. Rectification will likely fail or crop to the wrong rectangle — a screenshot is full of them. NOTE THE YEAR: the PSA label reads '2024 OBSIDIAN', a single year, which contradicts the season convention used for the Topps Chrome fixtures; the label is authoritative for a graded card. certNumber matters most here — it is looked up against PSA's API, so a wrong one returns a different card's grade and population. Its label abbreviates the year to '2024' while the Wembanyama slab abbreviates a 2023-24 product to '2023' — PSA's year field is not a consistent convention, so it is not a reliable source for this field.

2023-24 Topps Chrome rookie, San Antonio Spurs, PSA MINT 9. SCREENSHOT OF CARDPOP'S OWN LISTING PAGE — and that makes it the weakest of the fixtures as a test of card reading: the page displays 'Victor Wembanyama', '2023-24 Topps Chrome Basketball', 'NBA', '#1', 'Rookie Card (RC)', 'Base' and 'PSA 9' as text, so a model can score full marks without looking at the card at all. Useful for confirming screenshots don't break the pipeline; not evidence about reading cards. The photo inside is a genuine hand-held shot of the slab against a cluttered bedroom background. The PSA label reads '2023 TOPPS CHROME' but the product is the 2023-24 season — asserted as the season per the agreed convention. Base card, so no insert or parallel. The RC shield is printed on the card front and the listing page shows the Rookie Card (RC) chip, so `rookie` is asserted.

2023-24 Panini Donruss Net Marvels, Red Laser parallel, PSA GEM MT 10. FIRST TWO-IMAGE FIXTURE, and the first that genuinely needs the back: 'No. 9' and the copyright line '2023-24 PANINI - DONRUSS BASKETBALL' are only legible there. Every earlier fixture noted its number as unreadable — this one tests whether sending the back actually recovers it. ADVERSARIAL BACKGROUND: two other PSA slabs are in frame behind the card, including a Donruss Wembanyama PSA 9 whose own label and cert are partly legible, so there is a real chance of reading the wrong card's details. Year asserted as the season per the card's own copyright, not the '2023 DONRUSS' on the flip. Parallel asserted as 'Red Laser'; the flip abbreviates it to 'NET MARVELS-RED'. Note the GG Jackson fixture calls its parallel 'Red Laser Holo' — if these turn out to be the same family named differently, one of the two expectations needs revising.

2023-24 Panini Mosaic Pictographs on-card autograph, numbered 08/25, Philadelphia 76ers. THE AUTOGRAPH FIXTURE — a real blue on-card signature over a sticker window, which is what the Auto chip and the isAuto flag exist for. Also the first non-numeric collector number ('No. PM-RCF' on the back, an insert code with a hyphen) and the first printed serial ('08/25'), which should imply the Numbered chip on its own. Front is upside-down and heavily glare-speckled by the mosaic foil under rigid plastic; the back carries the number, the serial and the '2023-24 PANINI - MOSAIC BASKETBALL' copyright, so this is a genuine two-image case. The RC shield is on the front bottom-right. `variants` now includes 'Mosaic', derived deterministically from the product name by `productFinishNames` rather than read off the card — every card in Panini Mosaic carries the mosaic pattern, so it is a fact about the product, not a treatment the model has to spot. (The back also prints 'PRIZM'; that is not asserted, because the product is Mosaic.) `parallel` is unasserted: /25 is a limited parallel but its name is not printed.

THE FIRST POKEMON FIXTURE — until this case the entire TCG path was unmeasured and every fixture was NBA. Wizards-era Team Rocket Dark Charmeleon, non-holo Uncommon (the rarity symbol beside '32/82' is a diamond), unlimited print run. Exercises everything the sports fixtures cannot: the pokemon CardSight segment instead of a sports one, a '32/82' number whose set total matters (cardNumbersMatch compares the total, so 32/82 must not match 32/132), and a set name with no manufacturer word in it. The photo is rotated 90 degrees — the card is portrait but the frame is landscape, so the text runs bottom-to-top — and it is held in a hand over a stack of other cards, which is the realistic seller photo the rectification step exists for. `year` is '1999-2000' because that is the copyright range printed on the card ('(c)1999-2000 Wizards'); see the README note, this is a convention call, not a release date. `variants` asserts an EMPTY set deliberately: nothing on this card warrants a chip, so an empty list is the assertion that catches the pipeline inventing a Pokemon finish the way it once invented Refractor on a Donruss card. 'Unlimited' is a real chip and factually correct here, but it is derived from the ABSENCE of a 1st Edition stamp, which the OCR prompt forbids the model from inferring — so it is deliberately not asserted. If the pipeline does return 'Unlimited', that is an expectation question, not a failure. `rarity` is not a scored field, so Uncommon is recorded here only.

THE DISTRACTOR FIXTURE — a second card is visible at the right edge of the frame, and its own collector number '29/82' is legible. No other fixture tests this: the pipeline must read the SUBJECT card's number (92/132) and not a neighbouring card's, and 29/82 is a plausible-looking wrong answer from a different set entirely. A wrong cardNumber reaches a live listing, so this is exactly the failure mode worth measuring. Also the first apostrophe in a card name, which is why normalizeName carries a compact-name comparison ("Misty's Staryu" must not lose to "mistys staryu"); the same fix that made Farfetch'd work. Common rarity (filled circle beside the number), non-holo, illustrated by Ken Sugimori, Gym Challenge. Rotated 90 degrees like the Dark Charmeleon case, held over a stack. `year` is '1999-2000' from the printed '(c)1999-2000 Wizards' copyright. Note the user described this card as released in 2000, which is true of Gym Challenge, but the release year is NOT printed on the card — asserting it would require exactly the product knowledge the prompt bans. See the README. `variants` is an empty set: this card is non-holo and carries no attribute chip, so any chip returned is an invention.

Second Team Rocket card, and deliberately a near-duplicate of dark-charmeleon-team-rocket-unlimited: same set, same Uncommon diamond, same '(c)1999-2000 Wizards' copyright, same non-holo, same 90-degree rotation and hand-held framing. It is here for two narrow reasons rather than broad coverage. SAME-SET DISCRIMINATION: 39/82 and 32/82 differ only in the card number within one 82-card set, so a pipeline that anchors on the set and guesses the number has two fixtures that catch it. NAME PREFIX: 'Dark Kadabra' must not be satisfied by 'Kadabra' — the Wizards-era 'Dark' prefix is part of the card's identity and a different card entirely, which is what namesMatch's no-containment rule protects. Adds sample size to the Pokemon measurement but no new card *type* — it is not holo, not graded, not first edition, and has no distractor card in frame. The remaining Pokemon gaps after this are a holo, a graded slab, and a genuine 1st Edition stamp. `year` and the empty `variants` follow the same reasoning as the other two Pokemon cases; see the README.

THE YEAR DISCRIMINATOR, and the most load-bearing Pokemon case so far. This card's copyright is a SINGLE year — '(c)1995, 96, 98 Nintendo, Creatures, GAMEFREAK. (c)1999 Wizards' — whereas the three other Pokemon fixtures all print the range '(c)1999-2000 Wizards'. So `year` is '1999', not '1999-2000', and normalizeSeason keeps those distinct. With three fixtures expecting the range, a pipeline that pattern-matches 'Wizards-era Pokemon means 1999-2000' would score them all correct and only fail here — which is exactly the fabrication mode the releaseYear rule exists to prevent (a 2025-26 card once came back '2021-22'). SECOND, and subtler: Base Set cards carry NO set symbol. Nothing on this card says 'Base Set'. The only on-card clues are the number '63/102' and the 1999 copyright, so resolving the set REQUIRES the catalogue grounding step to look it up by card number — the model is forbidden from supplying it from product knowledge. This is the first fixture where setName has no readable source at all, making it a direct test of groundAgainstCatalogue rather than of OCR. THIRD, 'Base Set' is the literal set name behind the setsMatch substring guard: plain containment made it match 'Base Set 2', a different set that would then corroborate it. A real card now exercises that guard. Also the first /102 set total and the first bare Pokemon name — no 'Dark' or "Misty's" prefix — so it checks the pipeline does not over-prefix. Common (filled circle), non-holo, unlimited (thick yellow border, no 1st Edition stamp, not shadowless), illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita. Rotated 90 degrees, hand-held. `variants` is an empty set for the same reason as the other Pokemon cases: any chip returned is an invention.
